prompt: Explain how a refrigerator works, step by step, for a curious ten-year-old.
method: xctrace Metal System Trace, metal-gpu-intervals (GPU start / end per command buffer; Metal gives no per-dispatch times). normal: the engine's decode step at MLX defaults. split: mx.async_eval at every matmul's input and output, MLX_MAX_OPS_PER_BUFFER / MB unlimited, so each op group is exactly one command buffer, mapped to its group in submission order
notes:
Where one decode step's GPU time goes, op group by op group, and where the GPU waits (one request, greedy).

Two kinds of step, recorded in one process under Instruments' Metal System Trace (xctrace, ships with Xcode):
- normal: the engine's own decode step, untouched. Its GPU command buffers (each covers several ops; Metal does not
  report per-dispatch times) and the idle gaps between them are the "reality" timeline.
- split: the same step with every matmul's input and output evaluated on its own (mx.eval), so each op group gets
  its own command buffer(s) and a measured GPU start / end. Groups: norms+misc, in_proj, attention (full layers) or
  conv+gated-delta (DeltaNet layers), out_proj, mlp_up_gate_act, mlp_down, lm_head+sampling (everything after the
  last layer's MLP, including state writes). The extra syncs add idle time and remove overlap, so the split step is
  for per-op GPU durations only; its gaps are not the real ones.
GPU intervals are matched to op groups by time: each mx.eval is synchronous, so its GPU work lies inside its host
window. The host-to-trace clock offset is the one that puts the most intervals inside a window (reported).

Also runs the same normal steps once without xctrace (untraced wall time), so tracing distortion is visible.

    .venv/bin/python tools/mlx_step_trace.py --model <mlx 9B dir> --out results/mlx/step_trace_qwen35_9b/r1.json
